texts: The Stilllight Station is the lantern-station at the Sunken Cove.
The Stilllight Station is a demanding station.
Every Keeper fears the Stilllight Station.

mixed: the kind and the place come through (Stilllight Station is a lantern-station, located at the Sunken Cove), but the definite predicate 'the lantern-station' — the claim that it is the one and only lantern-station there — has no carrier in the instruction set, so the parse records only that it is *a* lantern-station. If that uniqueness is part of what you mean, write 'Only the Stilllight Station is a lantern-station at the Sunken Cove.'; if it is not, 'The Stilllight Station is a lantern-station at the Sunken Cove.' gives the same parse as now with nothing lost.
good. the name, the station kind and the evaluative 'demanding' each land as their own atom, with nothing invented.
good. parses as a fireable universal rule — one fearing state per Keeper, with the Stilllight Station as what is feared and the 'every' quantifier recorded.
Keepers visit the tide-pools at harvest time.
good. parses as a fireable generic rule — each Keeper gets their own visit, with the tide-pool group as what is visited and 'harvest time' kept as the time of the visit.
Keepers keep the lanterns at the Hollows dim.

good. the maintenance reading comes through as a fireable generic about what Keepers do, plus the reified 'dim' state, its continuation tag and a per-lantern rule so an individual lantern still answers 'is it dim?'; the reviewer's one objection about the dimness being asserted too strongly was overruled on adjudication. Note only that 'at the Hollows' was attached to the lanterns (the lanterns that are at the Hollows), not to the keeping.
The Stilllight Station is a hard station.

good. the multi-word name becomes one symbol with its name record, the kind word is stated once as the station's type, and "hard" is carried as a separate property of that station rather than being fused into a kind of its own — nothing in the sentence is dropped or added.
Each Keeper checks the lantern at midnight.
Each Keeper checks the lantern at the third watch.

good. the bare plural reads as a generic and becomes a fireable rule that gives every night shift its own beginning, with "shift" exposed as the genus of night_shift and "at sundown" kept as that beginning's time.

good. "each Keeper" distributes into a fireable per-keeper rule, the quantifier word is recorded, the definite "the lantern" is one shared object asserted outside the rule, and "at midnight" is kept as the time of each check. keeping the singular kind word here ("each Keeper") is what lets the rule bind actual keepers.

good. same fireable per-keeper rule as the midnight version, with "the third watch" kept as a named time constant — the licensed route for an ordinal-named period — so no content is lost by the unusual time expression.
Every first-year apprentice wears an unstained coat.

good. the universal becomes a fireable rule giving each first-year apprentice their own coat, "unstained" rides on that coat as a property rather than being fused into a kind, and the quantifier word is recorded alongside the rule.
A few Keepers keep a notebook of moth-counts and weather notes.
Whenever an heir inherits a Keeper's lantern-station, that heir inherits that Keeper's notebook.

(: heir_inherit_whenever (Implication (And (Member $h heir) (Member $k keeper) (Member $e inherit) (Agent $e $h) (Theme $e $ls) (Member $ls lantern_station) (Possession $ls $k)) (And (Member (sk_inherit_notebook $h $k) inherit) (Agent (sk_inherit_notebook $h $k) $h) (Theme (sk_inherit_notebook $h $k) (sk_notebook $k)) (Member (sk_notebook $k) notebook) (Possession (sk_notebook $k) $k) (During (sk_inherit_notebook $h $k) $e))) (STV 1.0 0.9))

bad: two things go wrong. The parse hands every one of the few Keepers the *same single* notebook instead of one notebook each, and the whole "of moth-counts and weather notes" phrase is dropped, so nothing records what the notebook holds (an of-phrase naming a thing's contents has no carrier in our instruction set). Make the per-Keeper reading explicit and turn the contents into a finite clause: "A few Keepers each keep a notebook that lists moth-counts and weather notes."

mixed: the rule is fireable and says the right thing for any one inheritance, but the derived notebook-inheritance is keyed to the heir and the Keeper rather than to the triggering occasion, so two separate station-inheritances by the same heir from the same Keeper would collapse into a single notebook-inheritance. The sentence is already in the shape we recommend (one finite clause per condition, explicit subjects, "that heir"/"that Keeper" pointing back cleanly), so no rewrite would help here — keep it as written; the fault is on our side and clears on a re-parse.
Whenever a Keeper leaves a station, the Council assigns an apprentice to that station.
Whenever an apprentice completes thirty solo nights, the Council assigns that apprentice to a station.

(: whenever_leave_assign (Implication (And (Member $e leave) (Agent $e $k) (Theme $e $s) (Member $k keeper) (Member $s station)) (And (Member (sk_assign $k $s) assign) (Agent (sk_assign $k $s) sk_council_1) (Theme (sk_assign $k $s) (sk_apprentice $k $s)) (Member (sk_apprentice $k $s) apprentice) (Goal (sk_assign $k $s) $s) (During (sk_assign $k $s) $e))) (STV 1.0 0.9))

(: apprentice_station_rule (Implication (And (Member $a apprentice) (Member $e complete) (Agent $e $a) (Theme $e $g) (GroupOf $g solo_night) (Cardinality $g 30)) (And (Member (sk_assign $e) assign) (Agent (sk_assign $e) sk_council_1) (Theme (sk_assign $e) $a) (Goal (sk_assign $e) (sk_station $e)) (Member (sk_station $e) station) (During (sk_assign $e) $e))) (STV 1.0 0.9))

mixed: every participant and role is captured and the rule fires, but the assignment and the apprentice are keyed to the Keeper and the station rather than to the triggering departure, so two departures of the same Keeper from the same station would yield one assignment and one apprentice instead of one per occasion. The wording is already the recommended "Whenever X, Y" form with explicit subjects and one finite clause per event, so no rewrite would improve it — keep the sentence as written; the fix is on our side.
good. parses as a fireable rule keyed to each qualifying occasion, with the thirty solo nights counted as a group, the Council as the assigner, and a station supplied per occasion.
Keepers rarely take apprentices from outside Keeper families.

good. parses as a fireable generic rule at the low strength "rarely" calls for, with the word itself recorded, and it keeps the "from outside Keeper families" restriction attached to the apprentice rather than dropping it.
Every Keeper considers that lantern-tending is sacred.

good. the universal over Keepers becomes a fireable rule that gives each Keeper a considering of its own, and the sacredness claim is held as a sealed opinion rather than asserted as a fact of the world, which is exactly what 'considers that' says. The only loose end is on our side (which base form the compound 'lantern-tending' should decompose to); no content of the sentence is lost.
Whenever a birth takes place, a Keeper repeats the phrase.
Whenever a funeral takes place, a Keeper repeats the phrase.
Whenever the Council closes a session, a Keeper repeats the phrase.

(: lorep19_whenever_rule (Implication (And (Member $x close) (Agent $x sk_council_1) (Patient $x $s) (Member $s session)) (And (Member (sk_repeat $x) repeat) (Agent (sk_repeat $x) (sk_keeper $x)) (Member (sk_keeper $x) keeper) (Theme (sk_repeat $x) sk_phrase_1) (During (sk_repeat $x) $x))) (STV 1.0 0.9))
good. 'takes place' correctly adds no separate happening of its own, and the rule fires on any birth, giving that occasion its own Keeper and its own repeating, timed to the birth.
good. same shape as the birth sentence and equally fireable: any funeral triggers a repeating by a Keeper on that occasion, with 'the phrase' kept as one shared thing across the item.

good. both halves of the trigger (the Council as the closer, a session as what is closed) are matched by open variables, so the rule fires on any recorded session-closing, and the response repeating is tied to it.
The two barred Keepers often neglected the Stilllight Station.

bad: the parse gives each of the two barred Keepers a separate neglecting but drops the pair-level fact the sentence also states, so a question asked about the two Keepers together (rather than about one of them) finds nothing, and the group that carries the count of two never takes part in any event. Making the distribution explicit removes that double-record requirement, since an explicit universal is recorded only per member: 'Each of the two barred Keepers often neglected the Stilllight Station.' That keeps the count, the 'barred' restriction, the 'often', and the station's name intact, and leaves exactly the per-Keeper reading the original intends.
The village pays each Keeper in food and shelter.

(: village_pays_keeper (Implication (Member $x keeper) (And (Member (sk_pay $x) pay) (Agent (sk_pay $x) sk_village_1) (Recipient (sk_pay $x) $x) (Instrument (sk_pay $x) food) (Instrument (sk_pay $x) shelter))) (STV 1.0 0.9))

good. the sentence lands as one fireable rule that gives each Keeper their own payment, with the village as the payer, the Keeper as the one paid, and food and shelter both recorded as what the payment is made in; the 'each' is kept as an explicit quantifier, and no content is dropped or duplicated into two separate payment events.

good. the Council is recorded as a specific body (correctly with no proper-name treatment), the seven elders as a counted group, and the having relation ties them together, so both 'what does the Council have?' and 'how many elders?' resolve.

good. parses as a fireable general rule that gives every council member a term of service marked as permanent, at the usual generic reliability. One note that needs no rewrite: 'Council members' becomes its own kind label, so it does not automatically join up with 'the Council' of the previous sentence; wording it as 'every member of the Council' would not fix that either, since each sentence is parsed on its own — the linking is a knowledge-base matter, not a fault of this sentence.
Every vote is decided by a simple majority.

good. every vote gets its own deciding, with the vote as the thing decided and its own simple majority as what decides it, the 'every' kept as an explicit quantifier, and 'simple majority' unpacked as a kind of majority; the rule is fireable on any vote the knowledge base later mentions.
The Stilllight Station draws mire-essence from the central pool.

good. the station comes through as one named entity with its kind, mire-essence stays a mass substance linked to essence, and the drawing event keeps the pool as its source, so "what does the Stilllight Station draw, and where from?" resolves.
The Council reads letters from neighbouring villages aloud.

bad: the clause has no tense marker, so it reads as a standing practice, and the two bare plurals then force the parse to invent one particular batch of letters and one particular set of villages that the sentence never claims exist; if the object instead falls back to the bare kind "letter", there is nowhere left to attach "from neighbouring villages" and the restriction is lost. Put the restricted plural in subject position so the restriction becomes part of the generalization itself: "Letters from neighbouring villages are read aloud by the Council." That version says exactly the same thing (any letter whose origin is a neighbouring village gets read aloud by the Council) while keeping the Council, the reading-aloud manner and the origin restriction all encoded, and it posits no specific letters or villages.
The Council doubled the feather ration of the Stilllight Station twenty-six years ago.
Sixty-three years ago, Old Vesh's father walked the Cove Stair every evening with three Keepers.

good. the Council stays an unnamed body, "Stilllight Station" is one named entity carrying its station kind, the feather ration is tied to that station, and "twenty-six years ago" is stored as a measured 26-year gap back from now, so the doubling is both past-tensed and datable.

good. every piece lands: the sixty-three-year gap, the father tied to Old Vesh, the Cove Stair as a named place, the walking as a past nightly habit (evening slot plus a daily cycle), and the three Keepers as a counted group of companions on the walk. Note only that the Keepers travel as one three-member companion group, so questions about a single named Keeper's walk will not resolve from this sentence alone.
Keepers from Aelmere exchange letters with the lantern-keepers of Faltern.
Villages on this coast do not keep lanterns.

(: keepers_exchange (Implication (And (Member $x keeper) (From $x aelmere)) (And (Member (sk_exchange $x) exchange) (Agent (sk_exchange $x) $x) (Agent (sk_exchange $x) sk_lkeepers_1) (Theme (sk_exchange $x) letter))) (STV 0.9 0.9))

mixed: the exchange, both villages and the Faltern group all come through, but "lantern-keepers" is welded into one kind symbol that is recorded only as a kind of keeper - nothing in the parse says these keepers keep lanterns, so "who keeps lanterns in Faltern?" finds nothing there. Say it in its own clause: "Keepers from Aelmere exchange letters with the keepers of Faltern, who keep lanterns." One caveat that is our fault rather than your wording: "exchange ... with" between a whole class (any Keeper from Aelmere) and one definite group (the Faltern keepers) has no settled shape in our instruction set yet, so that half of the parse may come out differently on a re-parse.
good. the "on this coast" restriction survives as a condition on the rule rather than being dropped, and the denial covers the whole keeping predication.
good. a plain habitual keeping event with Aelmere as the doer and lanterns as a non-specific object, and no kind invented for Aelmere that the sentence does not state.
Each Keeper eats a small meal at sundown before the shift.
Each apprentice walks to the station with a senior Keeper.

(: keeper_eat_rule (Implication (Member $x keeper) (And (Member (sk_eat $x) eat) (Agent (sk_eat $x) $x) (Patient (sk_eat $x) (sk_meal $x)) (Member (sk_meal $x) meal) (Member (sk_meal $x) small) (Time (sk_eat $x) sundown) (Member (sk_shift $x) shift) (Before (sk_eat $x) (sk_shift $x)))) (STV 1.0 0.9))
good. a fireable generic rule, with "during the day" kept as the time of each sleeping.

mixed: the rule, the small meal and the sundown timing are all right, but "the shift" is minted fresh for every Keeper inside the rule instead of standing as one specific shift outside it, so nothing at top level says the shift exists and the before-relation cannot be queried against it. That part is our fault and clears on a re-parse. Worth knowing, though: the compliant reading of "the shift" is ONE shift shared by every Keeper - if you mean each Keeper's own shift, say so: "Each Keeper eats a small meal at sundown, before that Keeper's shift begins."
good. each apprentice gets their own walk and their own senior Keeper as companion, with the station shared, which is the right reading of "each ... with a ...".
Replacement lanterns need no Council touch.

mixed: every atom is true and the parse was judged compliant, but two parts of the wording sit in corners our instruction set does not cover - "Council touch" fuses into one kind symbol whose "council" half is deliberately not exposed, so nothing links this claim to the Council itself, and an object-position "no" has no defined route, so the word is consumed into the rule's falsity and leaves no trace. Rewriting costs you nothing on either count: "Replacement lanterns do not need a touch from the Council." - the negation then sits on the verb, where it is fully specified, and the Council becomes a referent your other Council sentences can join to.
Wicks carbonize over a long burn.

good. parses as a fireable generic rule: every wick gets its own carbonizing event tied to its own long burn by the plain "over" relation, with "long" kept as a property of the burn and no wick-burn link invented.
The village holds a feast at Mid-summer during peak moth-season.
good. the village, the feast, the Mid-summer date and the peak-moth-season window are all carried, with "during" kept as the stated relation and no recurrence or extra link invented.
When a Keeper marries into a fisher family, that Keeper keeps the station.

(: keeper_marry_keep_rule (Implication (And (Member $k keeper) (Member $m marry) (Agent $m $k) (Goal $m $f) (Member $f fisher_family)) (And (Member (sk_keep $m) keep) (Agent (sk_keep $m) $k) (Theme (sk_keep $m) sk_station_1) (During (sk_keep $m) $m))) (STV 1.0 0.9))

mixed: the rule itself fires correctly — each Keeper who marries into a fisher family gets a keeping-the-station event tied to that marriage — but "marries into a fisher family" is recorded with a spatial destination role, as though the Keeper travelled to the family, instead of the plain "into" relation, which distorts the marriage-alliance sense. Giving the marriage an ordinary object removes the prepositional verb: "When a Keeper marries a member of a fisher family, that Keeper keeps the station."

good. the permission lands as a kind-level norm on keeper_child and "decline apprenticeship" is unpacked, so "what may they decline?" answers; note that the capitalized "Keeper" is read as an ordinary modifier fused into the kind symbol, so the parse itself carries no link back to the Keeper class.
Every Keeper believes that the dead of the storm-surge became wraiths.

(: keeper_believe_rule (Implication (Member $k keeper) (And (Member (sk_believe $k) believe) (Experiencer (sk_believe $k) $k) (Theme (sk_believe $k) (And (Possession sk_group_1 sk_storm_surge_1) (Member sk_become_1 become) (Patient sk_become_1 sk_group_1) (Past sk_become_1) (Member sk_wraith_1 wraith) (Experiencer sk_wraith_1 sk_group_1) (Result sk_become_1 sk_wraith_1) (Implication (PartOf $x sk_group_1) (Member $x wraith)))))) (STV 1.0 0.9))

mixed: the belief, the quantification over every Keeper and the becoming-wraiths are all captured and the rule fires, but "the dead of the storm-surge" has no licensed relation, so the parse falls back on a loose possession link that says only that the dead are somehow the surge's, never that the surge killed them. Say the dying outright: "Every Keeper believes that the people who died in the storm-surge became wraiths." That gives a real dying event tied to the surge, and the rest of the parse (the belief rule, the change into wraiths, the per-member distribution) stays exactly as it is.
Wraiths drain mire-essence from lit lanterns.
Keepers have known the wraith rule for generations.

(: wraith_drain (Implication (Member $x wraith) (And (Member (sk_drain $x) drain) (Agent (sk_drain $x) $x) (Patient (sk_drain $x) mire_essence) (Source (sk_drain $x) (sk_lantern $x)) (Member (sk_lantern $x) lantern) (Member (sk_lantern $x) lit))) (STV 0.9 0.9))

(: keepers_know_rule (Implication (Member $x keeper) (And (Member (sk_know $x) know) (Experiencer (sk_know $x) $x) (Stimulus (sk_know $x) sk_wraith_rule_1) (Ongoing (sk_know $x)) (MeasureAtLeast (sk_know $x) duration 2 generation))) (STV 0.9 0.9))

mixed: the denial is recorded faithfully, but as one opaque kind-to-kind atom at strength 0 — having bare kind words ("wraiths", "people") on both sides is what selects that form — and such an atom never reaches individuals, so asking whether THIS wraith harms someone comes back unknown instead of no. If you want the denial to carry down to each wraith, write "No wraith harms people." — the explicit quantifier forces the per-wraith rule form, which hands the strength-0 result to every wraith the reasoner knows about.

mixed: the rule fires and keeps the from-the-lantern link, but the mire-essence is filed as something the draining creates or changes when draining only moves it out of the lantern, and the plural "lit lanterns" shrinks to a single lantern per wraith. The wording that removes the doubt is "Wraiths siphon mire-essence from lit lanterns." — siphoning reads unmistakably as a transfer, so the essence lands in the moved-not-changed slot. The lantern plural has no better carrier in the current instruction set, so expect that narrowing to remain either way.

good. the "drained" restriction rides as a premise condition rather than being fused into the lantern's kind, and "dimly" keeps its surface adverb form. One side effect of the generic-rule shape: it also asserts that drained lanterns do burn, where the sentence only characterizes how they burn.

mixed: this becomes a per-Keeper rule and then hangs "for generations" on each Keeper's own knowing, so it asserts that every individual Keeper has known the rule for two or more generations — which no one person can. Put the generations on the people instead of on one person's knowing: "Generations of Keepers have known the wraith rule." Avoid the form "The Keepers have known ...": a capitalized plural after "the" is read as a single named thing, which would cut the sentence off from the Keeper kind entirely.
Wraiths persist for several weeks before they fade back into the cove.
Persisting wraiths approach lit lanterns each night.
Wraiths drain many lanterns while they persist.

(: wraith_persist_fade (Implication (Member $x wraith) (And (Member (sk_persist $x) persist) (Experiencer (sk_persist $x) $x) (MeasureAtLeast (sk_persist $x) duration 2 week) (Member (sk_fade $x) fade) (Patient (sk_fade $x) $x) (Goal (sk_fade $x) sk_cove_1) (Before (sk_persist $x) (sk_fade $x)))) (STV 0.9 0.9))

(: lp46_rule (Implication (And (Member $x wraith) (Member $x persisting)) (And (Member (sk_approach $x) approach) (Agent (sk_approach $x) $x) (Theme (sk_approach $x) (sk_lantern $x)) (Member (sk_lantern $x) lantern) (Member (sk_lantern $x) lit) (Time (sk_approach $x) night) (Every (sk_approach $x) 1 day))) (STV 0.9 0.9))

good. the rule fires, with the persisting, its at-least-two-weeks span and the ordering before the fading into the cove all hung on the same wraith; the adjudicator confirmed that bound as a faithful reading of "several weeks". Only the word "several" itself and the "back" of "fade back" leave no trace in the atoms — an acknowledged hole in the instruction set, not something a rewrite of yours would fix.

good. the "persisting" restriction rides as a premise condition, both participles stay adjectives rather than turning into verbs, and "each night" is recorded as a nightly recurrence at night. The one narrowing worth knowing about: the plural "lit lanterns" comes out as at least one lit lantern per wraith rather than several — under-specified, not wrong.
good. the rule fires with the lanterns as a counted group carrying the word "many", and "while they persist" places the draining inside the persisting with no invented connective.
Each feather warding lasts about a month.

good. the compound kind (feather warding, still a kind of warding), the "each" quantifier and the hedged duration "about a month" all come through, and the rule is fireable, so a later question like "how long does a feather warding last?" resolves.
Keepers warded the wraith back with ground feathers.
Every Keeper considers that the plan was dangerous.

mixed: the warding event, "ward back" kept whole as one verb, the group of Keepers doing it, the wraith as what was warded, and the feathers as the means are all correct; the one bad atom is "ground", which lands on the bundle of feathers as a whole rather than on each feather, so "was this feather ground?" can never resolve. Moving the modifier into its own clause fixes it without changing what you are saying: "Keepers warded the wraith back with feathers that had been ground."

good. the opinion is recorded as every Keeper's own, the plan's dangerousness stays inside the belief (nothing asserts the plan really was dangerous), the past tense is kept there too, and the rule fires for any Keeper who turns up later.
A few Keepers believe that a wraith remembers the Keeper who let that wraith rise.

(: grp_believe_theme (Theme sk_believe_1 (And (Member sk_wraith_1 wraith) (Member sk_remember_1 remember) (Experiencer sk_remember_1 sk_wraith_1) (Stimulus sk_remember_1 sk_keeper_1) (Member sk_let_1 let) (Agent sk_let_1 sk_keeper_1) (Theme sk_let_1 sk_rise_1) (Past sk_let_1) (Member sk_rise_1 rise) (Agent sk_rise_1 sk_wraith_1))) (STV 1.0 0.99))

(: keeper_believe_rule (Implication (PartOf $x sk_group_1) (And (Member (sk_believe $x) believe) (Experiencer (sk_believe $x) $x) (Theme (sk_believe $x) (And (Member sk_wraith_1 wraith) (Member sk_remember_1 remember) (Experiencer sk_remember_1 sk_wraith_1) (Stimulus sk_remember_1 sk_keeper_1) (Member sk_let_1 let) (Agent sk_let_1 sk_keeper_1) (Theme sk_let_1 sk_rise_1) (Past sk_let_1) (Member sk_rise_1 rise) (Agent sk_rise_1 sk_wraith_1))))) (STV 1.0 0.9))

mixed: "a few Keepers" gives a properly counted group with both a group belief and a per-Keeper rule, and the belief content is correctly held unasserted (nothing claims a wraith really does remember). But "a wraith" with a verbal predicate reads as one particular wraith rather than the general rule you seem to mean, and because "the Keeper who let that wraith rise" is identified only inside the belief, the parse still asserts one specific Keeper at top level. Making the generality explicit and letting the pronoun bind puts it on the well-supported rule pattern: "A few Keepers believe that every wraith remembers the Keeper who let it rise."
good. both "Keepers" and "sky-cats" are bare plurals, so the sentence stores as one kind-level relation between the two kinds plus the sky-cat/cat genus, with nothing dropped and nothing invented.
Every sky-cat has broad feathered wings.
Keepers rarely witness a sky-cat hunt.

(: sky_cat_wing_rule (Implication (Member $x sky_cat) (And (Member (sk_have $x) have) (Holder (sk_have $x) $x) (Theme (sk_have $x) (sk_wings $x)) (Member (sk_wings $x) wing) (Member (sk_wings $x) broad) (Member (sk_wings $x) feathered))) (STV 1.0 0.9))

bad: a plural object carrying descriptive adjectives ("broad feathered wings") under "every" has no faithful form in our translator — the parse types the pair of wings as a single wing and hangs "broad" and "feathered" on the wing-collection rather than on each wing, so the description is distorted. Split the possession from the description: "Every sky-cat has wings. Sky-cat wings are broad and feathered." The first sentence keeps the universal and the second states both properties as an ordinary generic about sky-cat wings, which needs no plural machinery at all.

bad: "a sky-cat hunt" is a noun compound the translator cannot unpack faithfully — it invented a role making the sky-cat the thing hunted, and the phrase is genuinely ambiguous between a hunt BY a sky-cat and a hunt OF one; "witness" additionally pushed the keeper onto the wrong subject role. State the hunting as a clause with an explicit hunter: "Keepers rarely see a sky-cat hunting." That keeps the rarity and the perceiving, and see-plus-participle is a construction the instruction set spells out, so the sky-cat lands as the hunter and no unstated role atom appears.
Keepers cannot count the sky-cats exactly.

bad: with the bare plural "Keepers" this is a can-claim about the whole kind, which the translator must store as a bare inability property on "keeper" — a form with no slot for "the sky-cats" and none for "exactly", so both are dropped and the claim widens to "keepers cannot count sky-cats at all". Make the subject the specific set of keepers so the clause takes the ordinary event form, which carries the counted group and the adverb: "The keepers cannot count the sky-cats exactly."
Keepers have used the crowd rule for generations.

(: keepers_use_rule (Implication (Member $x keeper) (And (Member (sk_use $x) use) (Agent (sk_use $x) $x) (Theme (sk_use $x) sk_rule_1) (Ongoing (sk_use $x)) (MeasureAtLeast (sk_use $x) duration 2 generation))) (STV 0.9 0.9))

mixed: the generic rule itself is right (every Keeper gets a using-the-crowd-rule event, and it fires), but "for generations" cannot ride it — a generic sentence hands every atom to each individual Keeper, so the span comes out as "each Keeper used the crowd rule for at least two generations", which the sentence never claims; the span belongs to the practice across Keepers and there is no carrier for that, so it has to be dropped and the content is lost either way. Give the span its own finite clause with a singular subject so it attaches to the practice rather than to each Keeper: "Keepers use the crowd rule, and this practice has continued for generations."
Every Keeper considers that sky-cats are sacred.
Sky-cats sometimes carry a nightmoth to the spires in flight.

(: skycat_carry_rule (Implication (Member $x sky_cat) (And (Member (sk_carry $x) carry) (Agent (sk_carry $x) $x) (Theme (sk_carry $x) (sk_nightmoth $x)) (Member (sk_nightmoth $x) nightmoth) (Goal (sk_carry $x) sk_spire_1) (In (sk_carry $x) flight))) (STV 0.5 0.9))
good. the universal over Keepers parses as a fireable rule with the quantifier word recorded, and the belief is sealed under the considering event, so nothing asserts that sky-cats really are sacred.
good. "never" parses as the same per-Keeper rule at strength zero, with the sky-cat object varying per Keeper inside the rule; fireable, with nothing lost.
good. "sometimes" sets the rule's strength and is recorded as a quantifier, and the moth, the destination and "in flight" all land in the rule; fireable with every participant covered.
Keepers count the visible sky-cats on the cliff-spires each morning.
Keepers track the weight of the feather harvest.

(: keeper_count_rule (Implication (Member $x keeper) (And (Member (sk_count $x) count) (Agent (sk_count $x) $x) (Theme (sk_count $x) sk_group_1) (Time (sk_count $x) morning) (Every (sk_count $x) 1 day))) (STV 0.9 0.9))

Neap tides leave the tide-pools dry.

bad: 'leave the tide-pools dry' is a result-state clause whose object is a definite plural, sitting inside a generic claim about neap tides — so the parse had to bury the half that hands 'dry' to each individual pool inside the generic rule's own conclusion, where its variable is bound by nothing and it carries no truth value of its own. No placement of that half is licensed (at the top level it would assert every tide-pool dry unconditionally), so as parsed the dryness of any one pool never actually derives. Rewrite it as a property that holds under a stated condition: "Tide-pools are dry at neap tide." That is a single licensed atom — the property 'dry' on the tide-pool kind, with 'neap tide' as the condition — which the reasoner can hand to any pool during a neap tide; the only shift is that the pools are the kind rather than one definite set, and the tide is named as the condition instead of the grammatical subject.
